algorithm: UTF-8; object members sorted by UTF-16 code unit of the key; no whitespace; strings escaped as JSON.stringify does (quote, backslash, the five short escapes, lowercase \u00xx for other C0, lowercase \udxxx for an unpaired surrogate, everything else raw); numbers in ECMAScript Number::toString shortest round-tripping form.

accepted.note: Members are emitted in code-unit order of the key, not the order they were written.
Uppercase sorts before lowercase because U+005A < U+0061. A locale-aware sort would reverse these two.

An astral key (surrogate pair, first unit U+D83D) sorts BEFORE U+FFFF, because the comparison is over UTF-16 code units. A code-point comparison would order them the other way; Kotlin String.compareTo agrees with this vector.
Quote, backslash and the five short escapes; a C0 control as lowercase \u00xx; a solidus NOT escaped; non-ASCII emitted raw as UTF-8.
An astral character survives as a surrogate pair, emitted raw rather than escaped.
An unpaired surrogate is escaped as \udxxx. This is the one place a JSON writer must not emit raw bytes, because the result would not be valid UTF-8.
Integers have no decimal point and no exponent.

Four spellings of one number collapse to one canonical form. This is intended: the value is the same, so one digest is right. Note the -0 in the input is written as 0 here because -0 is refused outright (see negative-zero).
Shortest round-tripping decimal. 0.1 is not exactly representable and neither is its shortest form.
The upper threshold: at 1e21 the notation switches from plain decimal to exponent form, and the exponent carries an explicit +.
The lower threshold: at 1e-7 the notation switches to exponent form, without a leading zero in the exponent.
The largest finite double and the smallest denormal. Kotlin Double.toString does not produce these spellings; the ECMAScript algorithm does.
The last exactly-representable integer and the first that is not: 9007199254740993 parses to 9007199254740992.
A value above the safe-integer range is still finite and is emitted in exponent form.
null, the empty string and the empty array are three distinct values with three distinct encodings. A missing member is a fourth thing: it is not in the object at all.
The encoding of an object with an explicit null member differs from the encoding of an object without it, so the two cannot share a digest.
The two empty containers have no whitespace between their delimiters.
Nesting is preserved exactly; only member order and whitespace are normalized.
A control vector: text that looks duplicated but is inside a string value is not a duplicate member and must be accepted.
A control vector: the same member name in two different objects is not a duplicate. Duplicate detection is per object, not per document.

rejected.note: The one double whose canonical form describes a different value. JSON.stringify(-0) is "0", so -0 and 0 would share a digest while Object.is distinguishes them.
The same rule applies wherever the value sits, not only at the root.
The same member named twice. JSON.parse keeps the last and discards the first, so the document has two readings.
The same member named twice, the second time as an escape sequence. Comparing raw quoted slices would miss this; the names are compared after unescaping.
Duplicate detection reaches every object in the document, not only the root.
A number literal that overflows the double range parses to Infinity, which has no JSON encoding. It is refused rather than mapped to null.

Thirty-four nested arrays put the innermost container at depth 33, one past the canonical bound of 32. Thirty-three is accepted, which is why this vector uses thirty-four: the bound counts containers from the root at 0, not nesting levels from 1.
Text that is not JSON at all.
